item.title: 🟠 The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th)
item.description:
Why this matters: Early technical signal — worth a quick scan for issues that may become more important.

One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.



Source: SANS Internet Storm Center  |  Severity: Important  |  Age: 1d

item.title: 🟠 Compromised TLS Certificates
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237...



Source: Schneier on Security  |  Severity: Important  |  Age: 13d
